title: LEAN VENTURE
subtitle: An assumption canvas and validation backlog
scope: A fictional Archive Desk venture canvas. Six hypotheses are untested; no customers, sales, prices, demand validation, funding commitment or actual business forecast is supplied.

chapters.title: State the venture as a question.
chapters.lead: Archive Desk is a fictional service concept for keeping a source, a saved passage and its intended use connected. The planning question is whether a defined reader task warrants a separate offering.
chapters.body: Treat the canvas as a collection of linked hypotheses, not a completed business case. A coherent explanation can still be wrong about the problem, the buyer or the work required to deliver it.
chapters.subheading: Business intent / not a launch claim
chapters.detail: The next useful artifact is a bounded description of the task and the evidence that would change the team’s mind. No operating venture is established by this document.
chapters.question: What must be true before this concept deserves more resources?

records.label: Intent
records.prompt: Explore whether source-context work warrants an offering.

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: No actual venture, release or customer demand established.

records.label: Next artifact
records.prompt: A task description with explicit disconfirming questions.

chapters.title: Define a customer hypothesis without inventing a customer.
chapters.lead: The proposed customer is an organisation preparing source-based explanations. The person doing the work may differ from the person who could approve a purchase.
chapters.body: Separate user, buyer and authorising role. These are planning lenses, not researched segments or named organisations. A task that matters to a user does not automatically establish budget or a willingness to pay.
chapters.detail: Ask who experiences the task, who chooses an approach and who would need to review a commercial arrangement. Retain unknowns rather than filling the canvas with fictional endorsements.
chapters.question: Which role would need to see value before an actual purchase could be considered?

records.label: User hypothesis
records.prompt: A person preparing source-based explanatory material.

records.label: Buyer hypothesis
records.prompt: An organisation considering a defined support offering.

records.label: Evidence gap
records.prompt: No buyer interview, budget or purchase authority supplied.

chapters.title: Describe the problem narrowly.
chapters.lead: A passage can be easy to locate but difficult to interpret when its original question or source context is missing. That is the proposed problem, not a measured pattern of customer failure.
chapters.body: A suitable inquiry would examine how people currently recover context and when that effort matters. Do not assume that a recurring inconvenience is costly enough to support a business or that a new service is the best response.
chapters.detail: Check the existing practice before defining a solution. A clearer annotation or a conversation may be sufficient in some settings.
chapters.question: What observation would challenge the idea that a separate offering is needed?

records.label: Problem premise
records.prompt: The reason for saving a passage can become unclear.

records.label: Alternative
records.prompt: An improved existing note or handoff may be enough.

records.label: Validation question
records.prompt: When does the missing context materially affect the task?

chapters.title: Write a value proposition with a mechanism.
chapters.lead: The proposed offering helps organise a passage, its source and the question it is intended to support. Its intended value is inspectable context, not guaranteed accuracy or productivity.
chapters.body: Explain what the service would actually provide before claiming a benefit. The concept does not establish working software, specialist verification, integration or the right to reuse another person’s source material.
chapters.detail: Proposed statement: bring the source and the reason for a passage into one reviewable note. Verify any real delivery capability before adapting the wording.
chapters.question: Can the proposed mechanism be demonstrated without promising an unsupported outcome?

records.label: Offering
records.prompt: A reviewable note connecting passage, source and purpose.

records.label: Intended value
records.prompt: Make the context available for an appropriate reviewer.

records.label: Capability gap
records.prompt: No implemented service or verified outcome supplied.

chapters.title: Treat the channel as a testable route.
chapters.lead: An outline shared through an appropriate professional introduction is one possible route to a concept conversation. A short explanatory page is another. Neither is an established acquisition channel.
chapters.body: Define the question each route should answer. A channel test should distinguish permission to contact someone, delivery of a message, understanding of the offering and a genuine commercial discussion.
chapters.detail: No contact list, live destination, campaign result or acquisition cost is supplied. The source register records an untested channel hypothesis only.
chapters.question: What would show that this route reaches an appropriate decision context?

records.label: Proposed route
records.prompt: An appropriate introduction to the concept outline.

records.label: Observation sought
records.prompt: Whether the intended reader understands the offering.

records.label: Unknown
records.prompt: No reach, response, conversion or acquisition-cost data.

chapters.title: Separate revenue logic from revenue evidence.
chapters.lead: One possible commercial model is payment for a defined review-support engagement. The scope, buyer, price and conditions would need real agreement before any revenue claim.
chapters.body: The canvas contains no sales, subscriptions, contracts or cash receipts. Do not convert an interesting conversation into a customer, a proposed price into willingness to pay or an invoice idea into actual revenue.
chapters.detail: Investigate what work would be purchased and how an appropriate buyer would assess it. Unknown commercial information stays unknown.
chapters.question: What would constitute reviewable evidence of a real commercial commitment?

records.label: Revenue hypothesis
records.prompt: Payment for a clearly scoped support engagement.

records.label: Terms to establish
records.prompt: Scope, price, buyer responsibility and conditions.

records.label: Evidence boundary
records.prompt: No agreement, sale or revenue supplied.

chapters.title: Expose the work behind the offering.
chapters.lead: Delivery may require preparation, source-context handling, reviewer time and coordination. Each is a cost question even when no money has changed hands.
chapters.body: Map the work before guessing a margin. This example supplies no pay rates, software costs, tax assumptions or operating budget. A plausible price cannot establish viability without the relevant delivery and commercial information.
chapters.detail: Ask which resources are fixed for a planning window and which vary with an engagement. Keep effort estimates separate from actual spending and staffing commitments.
chapters.question: Which resource could constrain delivery even if interest were present?

records.label: Work required
records.prompt: Preparation, source handling, review and coordination.

records.label: Cost gap
records.prompt: No rates, actual spending or validated effort estimates.

records.label: Constraint question
records.prompt: Which role or input limits a suitable engagement?

chapters.title: Prioritise what could invalidate the canvas.
chapters.lead: The validation backlog should start with the assumptions that would make other planning work irrelevant. If the proposed task is not important enough, optimising a channel may be premature.
chapters.body: The six-item register marks customer, problem, value, channel, revenue and cost as untested. No interview, experiment or result has been completed in this example. Rank a learning question by its consequence, not its ease of presentation.
chapters.detail: Start with whether an appropriate person recognises the task and whether a credible existing alternative already meets it. Define suitable evidence before collecting it.
chapters.question: Which uncertainty should be resolved before the next layer of planning?

records.label: First question
records.prompt: Does the task warrant a separate offering?

records.label: Second question
records.prompt: Can the proposed mechanism address a meaningful gap?

records.label: Backlog boundary
records.prompt: Six untested hypotheses, no validated demand.

chapters.title: Set a revision rule before seeking confirmation.
chapters.lead: A planning rule might be: revise the offering if an appropriate review cannot distinguish its proposed value from a simpler existing practice. That rule is a proposal, not a statistical decision threshold.
chapters.body: Specify what evidence would be relevant, what remains inconclusive and who can interpret it within the actual setting. Avoid collecting only favourable anecdotes or treating absence of a response as proof of absence of need.
chapters.detail: No sample, time window or quantitative pass rate is supplied. Agree those details appropriately before using a real evaluation to make a consequential decision.
chapters.question: What finding would make you stop, narrow or substantially change the concept?

records.label: Revise condition
records.prompt: The separate offering adds no clear task value.

records.label: Inconclusive condition
records.prompt: Evidence does not address the defined task.

records.label: Decision boundary
records.prompt: No measured threshold or approved business decision.

chapters.title: Revise the canvas and preserve the reason.
chapters.lead: A useful revision records which hypothesis changed, the evidence considered and the consequences for the rest of the canvas. Do not silently rewrite the original premise to fit a preferred conclusion.
chapters.body: The current document remains an authored planning example. Six hypotheses are untested, and no real business outcome is reported. Use a new version to make future reasoning inspectable rather than to manufacture a story of inevitable progress.
chapters.detail: Keep the previous hypothesis beside its replacement. A more polished canvas does not automatically represent a better supported venture.
chapters.question: Which linked assumption must be reconsidered when this one changes?

records.label: Version record
records.prompt: Keep the prior premise and the reason for change.

records.label: Linked effects
records.prompt: Revisit buyer, delivery and commercial assumptions together.

records.label: Outcome boundary
records.prompt: No validated venture, forecast or funding commitment.

title: SCENARIO LEDGER
subtitle: A three-case driver and constraint ledger
scope: A fictional Edition Table planning model using arbitrary teaching points. Three demand cases share capacity 12; points are not currency, revenue, profit, cash flow or a real forecast.

chapters.title: Define the planning window and its limits.
chapters.lead: Edition Table is a fictional review-support concept. This ledger compares three demand assumptions within one unspecified teaching window, holding the model’s delivery capacity at twelve tasks.
chapters.body: The cases are not probabilities or forecasts. They illustrate how demand, a capacity ceiling and a simple point model interact. No actual period, customer pipeline, operating budget or financial statement is supplied.
chapters.detail: All teaching points are arbitrary and non-monetary. Keep the source register with the discussion so a reader can distinguish model arithmetic from business evidence.
chapters.question: What can this model answer, and what remains outside its scope?

records.label: Window
records.prompt: One unspecified teaching window, not a calendar forecast.

records.label: Cases
records.prompt: Demand 8, 12 and 16; capacity fixed at 12.

records.label: Unit boundary
records.prompt: Teaching points are not currency or actual profit.

chapters.title: Name the drivers before comparing totals.
chapters.lead: Delivered tasks equal the smaller of demand and capacity. Unmet tasks equal demand minus delivery when positive. Unused capacity equals capacity minus delivery.
chapters.body: The point model assigns four benefit points per delivered task and resource points of twelve fixed plus two per delivered task. Net points subtract resources from benefits; they are not an accounting or valuation measure.
chapters.detail: Holding a driver fixed is a modelling choice, not evidence that it is stable in real work. The model excludes timing, quality variation, payment and many other operating conditions.
chapters.question: Which assumption has the greatest effect on interpreting the case comparison?

records.label: Delivery rule
records.prompt: Delivered = min(demand, capacity).

records.label: Resource rule
records.prompt: 12 fixed + 2 points per delivered task.

records.label: Net rule
records.prompt: 4 × delivered − resource points; not monetary profit.

chapters.title: Read the baseline as an assumption.
chapters.lead: In the baseline, demand is twelve and capacity is twelve. Delivery is twelve, with no unmet demand and no unused model capacity.
chapters.body: Benefits total forty-eight teaching points; resources total thirty-six; net points are twelve. A positive net figure only describes the authored rules. It does not demonstrate a viable business or a margin available to spend.
chapters.detail: No actual demand or delivery is recorded. A fully used model capacity may conceal the absence of a reserve or the need for quality checks in a real operation.
chapters.question: What would make full utilisation unsuitable in an actual setting?

records.label: Demand / delivery
records.prompt: 12 requested, 12 delivered in the model.

records.label: Resource points
records.prompt: 12 fixed + 24 variable = 36.

records.label: Net points
records.prompt: 48 − 36 = 12; not cash or profit.

chapters.title: Examine the conservative demand case.
chapters.lead: With demand of eight and capacity of twelve, delivery is eight. Four units of capacity remain unused in the model, and unmet demand is zero.
chapters.body: Benefits are thirty-two teaching points and resources are twenty-eight, leaving four net points. Lower demand does not automatically reduce the model’s fixed resource requirement. No probability or actual shortfall is attached to this case.
chapters.detail: The case tests one lower demand assumption. It does not cover every adverse condition, such as a missing input, a longer task or an unplanned interruption.
chapters.question: Which fixed commitment would remain if the model demand fell?

records.label: Demand / delivery
records.prompt: 8 requested, 8 delivered.

records.label: Capacity balance
records.prompt: 4 unused, 0 unmet.

records.label: Point arithmetic
records.prompt: 32 benefit − 28 resource = 4 net points.

chapters.title: Inspect demand above the capacity ceiling.
chapters.lead: In the exploratory case, demand is sixteen but capacity remains twelve. Delivery is capped at twelve and four requested tasks remain unmet.
chapters.body: Benefits, resources and net points match the baseline because delivery has not increased: forty-eight, thirty-six and twelve. Higher assumed demand is not higher actual revenue, and it does not remove the delivery constraint.
chapters.detail: Unmet demand here is arithmetic, not an observed backlog or an invitation to accept work that cannot be responsibly delivered. Actual response options need appropriate review.
chapters.question: What would have to change before additional demand could become suitable delivery?

records.label: Demand / delivery
records.prompt: 16 requested, delivery capped at 12.

records.label: Unmet tasks
records.prompt: 16 − 12 = 4; no actual backlog.

records.label: Constraint effect
records.prompt: Net remains 12 teaching points, as in baseline.

chapters.title: Change one driver to inspect sensitivity.
chapters.lead: At demand twelve, capacities of ten, twelve and fourteen produce deliveries of ten, twelve and twelve. Extra capacity above demand remains unused rather than generating extra benefit points.
chapters.body: Under the same point rules, net points are eight, twelve and twelve. This comparison excludes any cost of changing capacity, so it cannot justify adding resources or choosing an investment.
chapters.detail: The source sensitivity register keeps the demand and point rules fixed. A real capacity change could alter many conditions at once.
chapters.question: Which omitted cost would matter before acting on this sensitivity result?

records.label: Capacity 10
records.prompt: Deliver 10; net 8 points; unmet 2.

records.label: Capacity 12
records.prompt: Deliver 12; net 12 points; no unused units.

records.label: Capacity 14
records.prompt: Deliver 12; net 12 points; unused 2.

chapters.title: Keep the constraint visible in the plan.
chapters.lead: A capacity number summarises an assumption. It does not explain staffing, task complexity, access needs, rework or the availability of source material.
chapters.body: The ledger holds capacity at twelve to expose its effect. Before applying a similar model, inspect what actually limits the work and which reserve or review conditions should be preserved. Do not infer that every unused unit is waste.
chapters.detail: No real staffing allocation or service commitment is supplied. The model cannot approve a workload or determine a safe or appropriate pace of work.
chapters.question: What does the capacity assumption leave unexplained?

records.label: Known model limit
records.prompt: Delivery cannot exceed 12 tasks.

records.label: Missing operating detail
records.prompt: Roles, task mix, reserve and source availability.

records.label: Planning boundary
records.prompt: No actual workload or staffing decision authorised.

chapters.title: Define triggers as review questions.
chapters.lead: A proposed trigger might be to review the plan when the model shows unmet demand or when actual task conditions differ from the assumptions. A trigger starts inquiry; it does not select a response automatically.
chapters.body: No real observation threshold or monitoring system is supplied. In practice, define the source, window and responsibility before treating a count as a reason for consequential action.
chapters.detail: A modelled unmet count of four is not an actual alert. Keep the calculation separate from any eventual operational signal.
chapters.question: What evidence would make the trigger relevant to a real decision?

records.label: Proposed trigger
records.prompt: A delivery constraint becomes relevant to the task.

records.label: Observation needed
records.prompt: Appropriate actual demand and task information.

records.label: Review route
records.prompt: Responsibility and response need real agreement.

chapters.title: Compare responses without declaring a winner.
chapters.lead: Possible responses include narrowing the accepted scope, changing the timing or investigating additional capacity. Each alters conditions that the simple ledger does not evaluate.
chapters.body: Do not choose a response solely because it raises net teaching points. Quality, permissions, accessibility, commercial terms and the effect on existing work may matter more than a model total.
chapters.detail: The ledger is a conversation aid. It provides neither procurement approval nor a business recommendation about real money or people.
chapters.question: Which response would require the most important missing information?

records.label: Scope option
records.prompt: Clarify what work can be considered.

records.label: Timing option
records.prompt: Review whether the window assumption is appropriate.

records.label: Capacity option
records.prompt: Investigate actual constraints and change costs first.

chapters.title: Record the version and the reason for change.
chapters.lead: A version record should retain the demand cases, capacity rule, point definitions and the question the comparison was meant to support. Preserve previous assumptions when changing a driver.
chapters.body: This version contains three authored cases and three sensitivity rows. It reports no actual operating or financial result. A revised model should identify what changed in the evidence rather than only displaying a new total.
chapters.detail: If the unit, window or delivery definition changes, reconsider comparisons with earlier versions. Similar-looking figures may no longer mean the same thing.
chapters.question: Can another reviewer reproduce the calculation and understand its limits?

records.label: Retain
records.prompt: Driver definitions, source rows and prior version.

records.label: Explain
records.prompt: Which assumption changed and why.

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: Teaching arithmetic, not an actual financial forecast.

title: SERVICE ECONOMICS
subtitle: A demand-capacity and unit-model workbook
scope: A fictional Review Sessions capacity model. Minutes and teaching credits are illustrative; credits are not currency, prices, revenue or profit, and no actual service, staffing or demand is supplied.

chapters.title: Define one service unit before doing arithmetic.
chapters.lead: The fictional service unit is one bounded document-review session lasting forty-five teaching minutes. It examines a passage and its source question, not the correctness of every claim in a document.
chapters.body: Specify what is included and what remains outside the unit. This workbook establishes no operating service, professional verification, appointment availability or commercial contract. A real service definition needs appropriate responsibility and scope.
chapters.detail: The model uses one arbitrary planning window. Neither the duration nor the resource assumptions are validated observations of actual work.
chapters.question: What must be clear before a request can count as one service unit?

records.label: Unit
records.prompt: One bounded review of a passage and source question.

records.label: Duration assumption
records.prompt: 45 teaching minutes per completed session.

records.label: Exclusion
records.prompt: No guarantee of correctness or full-document approval.

chapters.title: Keep demand assumptions separate from bookings.
chapters.lead: The three model demand cases contain six, eight and ten requested sessions. They are authored planning inputs, not a waiting list, booked work or a measure of customer interest.
chapters.body: An actual demand assessment would need a defined request, a relevant window and an appropriate source. Counting enquiries as completed work would conceal both uncertainty and the delivery constraint.
chapters.detail: Demand above the model’s capacity produces an unmet count, not automatic permission to shorten sessions or make commitments.
chapters.question: Which definition would distinguish a request from a confirmed suitable booking?

records.label: Lower case
records.prompt: 6 hypothetical requests.

records.label: Reference case
records.prompt: 8 hypothetical requests.

records.label: Higher case
records.prompt: 10 hypothetical requests, not actual bookings.

chapters.title: Derive capacity from the stated time assumptions.
chapters.lead: The model starts with four hundred and fifty available teaching minutes and reserves ninety. That leaves three hundred and sixty minutes for the defined service units.
chapters.body: At forty-five minutes each, floor of 360 divided by 45 gives eight sessions. The reserve is a modelling boundary, not spare time that the workbook authorises someone to consume. No actual staffing arrangement is supplied.
chapters.detail: Changing a unit’s duration or the reserve changes the model. Preserve the original assumption and examine whether the service scope would still be appropriate.
chapters.question: Which assumption must be checked before calling eight sessions feasible?

records.label: Available / reserve
records.prompt: 450 minutes less 90 reserved = 360.

records.label: Unit / capacity
records.prompt: 360 ÷ 45 = 8 whole sessions.

records.label: Feasibility boundary
records.prompt: No observed duration, staff availability or workload approval.

chapters.title: Map the work around the session.
chapters.lead: Before a session, clarify the passage and relevant source. During it, inspect the stated question. After it, retain an appropriately agreed note about what remains unresolved.
chapters.body: The time model does not separately measure preparation, coordination or follow-up. If those activities draw on the same available minutes, the capacity calculation must be revised rather than quietly treating them as free.
chapters.detail: The ninety-minute reserve is not an itemised estimate of all supporting work. Real delivery needs a more complete account of tasks and responsibilities.
chapters.question: Which supporting task could make the simple capacity assumption misleading?

records.label: Before
records.prompt: Clarify scope and source availability.

records.label: During
records.prompt: Review the bounded passage-question relationship.

records.label: After
records.prompt: Record the remaining question under an appropriate agreement.

chapters.title: Use a unit model without pretending it is money.
chapters.lead: Each completed session receives ten benefit credits and uses four variable resource credits. The unit contribution is six credits; fixed resources are twenty credits per teaching window.
chapters.body: Credits are arbitrary non-monetary quantities used to illustrate structure. Net credits equal six times completed sessions minus twenty. They are not prices, sales, wages, cash flow or profit.
chapters.detail: The smallest whole number covering the model’s fixed credits is ceiling of 20 divided by 6, which is four completed sessions. This is a teaching threshold, not a real financial break-even.
chapters.question: What evidence would be needed before constructing an actual commercial unit model?

records.label: Unit contribution
records.prompt: 10 − 4 = 6 teaching credits.

records.label: Window net
records.prompt: 6 × completed sessions − 20 fixed credits.

records.label: Teaching threshold
records.prompt: ceil(20 ÷ 6) = 4 sessions; not financial break-even.

chapters.title: Distinguish fixed assumptions from fixed obligations.
chapters.lead: The model holds twenty fixed credits and a ninety-minute reserve unchanged across the three cases. That is a comparison choice, not evidence of an actual obligation or a complete operating cost base.
chapters.body: A real service may have resources that change in steps, shared capacity or commitments outside the planning window. Identify those conditions before translating a simple unit model into a decision.
chapters.detail: There are no rent, salary, tax, technology or insurance figures in this workbook. Do not interpret the teaching total as an actual cost estimate.
chapters.question: Which supposedly fixed resource might change when the delivery arrangement changes?

records.label: Model assumption
records.prompt: 20 fixed teaching credits per window.

records.label: Time boundary
records.prompt: 90 minutes reserved in the capacity model.

records.label: Missing costs
records.prompt: No actual spending, rates or contractual obligations supplied.

chapters.title: Compare the three demand cases.
chapters.lead: Demand six, eight and ten produces delivery six, eight and eight under the capacity ceiling. Unmet counts are zero, zero and two. Unused service minutes are ninety, zero and zero.
chapters.body: Net teaching credits are sixteen, twenty-eight and twenty-eight. The higher demand case cannot raise delivery or net credits without changing another assumption. No actual utilisation or financial performance is reported.
chapters.detail: Service minutes are delivered sessions times forty-five. Unused service minutes exclude the ninety-minute reserve, which remains separate in every case.
chapters.question: Which total stops changing when the capacity ceiling is reached?

records.label: Lower case
records.prompt: 6 delivered; 90 unused service minutes; net 16.

records.label: Reference case
records.prompt: 8 delivered; 0 unused service minutes; net 28.

records.label: Higher case
records.prompt: 8 delivered; 2 unmet requests; net remains 28.

chapters.title: Treat quality as a condition, not an automatic output.
chapters.lead: Completing eight units in the model says nothing about the suitability or quality of an actual review. A capacity equation cannot establish whether a participant had enough context or support.
chapters.body: Do not shorten a session merely to make the arithmetic fit more requests. Consider task complexity, access arrangements and the agreed review boundary before changing the unit definition or reserve.
chapters.detail: The workbook provides no quality score, satisfaction result or validated duration. Any real trade-off requires relevant information and appropriate responsibility.
chapters.question: What could be lost if the unit were compressed without changing its scope?

records.label: Scope check
records.prompt: The task remains bounded and understandable.

records.label: Support check
records.prompt: Relevant access and review conditions are considered.

records.label: Evidence gap
records.prompt: No actual service-quality or duration observations supplied.

chapters.title: Build a validation checklist around the unknowns.
chapters.lead: Before using a similar model, examine the request definition, actual task duration, supporting work, appropriate reserve and commercial conditions. Each needs a source rather than a confident guess.
chapters.body: Validate the meaning of the unit before seeking a precise number. A carefully calculated result can still be irrelevant if the service scope or planning window has changed.
chapters.detail: Start with scope and responsibility, then inspect time and demand information. Only use actual financial inputs when they are available and appropriately defined.
chapters.question: Which unknown would most change the interpretation of the model?

records.label: Scope evidence
records.prompt: An agreed definition of the service and exclusions.

records.label: Time evidence
records.prompt: Appropriate observations of the full task, not just contact time.

records.label: Commercial evidence
records.prompt: Actual terms and costs; none supplied here.

chapters.title: Turn the workbook into operating questions.
chapters.lead: The useful questions are whether the unit is meaningful, whether the time boundary is defensible and what happens when suitable requests exceed capacity. The point model cannot answer those questions alone.
chapters.body: This document remains a fictional planning example. No actual service, pricing decision, staffing approval or profitability claim follows from its calculations. Record which source would be needed for a more consequential decision.
chapters.detail: Carry forward one uncertainty about scope, one about resources and one about demand. Keep the teaching calculation available for inspection without upgrading it into a forecast.
chapters.question: What should be learned before the service concept is developed further?

records.label: Scope question
records.prompt: What work is included and appropriately supported?

records.label: Resource question
records.prompt: What actually constrains delivery in the relevant setting?

records.label: Demand question
records.prompt: Which requests represent a suitable, defined need?

title: GROWTH OPTIONS
subtitle: An option portfolio and experiment sequence
scope: A fictional Field Editions option portfolio. Resource tokens are non-monetary teaching units; options, dependencies and learning rules are unvalidated, not growth forecasts or investment recommendations.

chapters.title: Define growth as a question about value.
chapters.lead: Field Editions is a fictional publishing-support concept. Its planning question is which adjacent task might be worth exploring without losing sight of the core explanation work.
chapters.body: Growth is not assumed to be desirable at any cost. The option portfolio organises learning choices and dependencies; it reports no current market, customer base or expansion result. A smaller or unchanged scope may remain appropriate.
chapters.detail: The five options use teaching tokens to illustrate resource constraints. Tokens are not money, approved budgets or expected returns.
chapters.question: What would make an expansion useful rather than merely larger?

records.label: Intent
records.prompt: Explore a task that adds appropriate reader value.

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: No actual market, customers or growth established.

records.label: Decision lens
records.prompt: Learn before expanding commitments.

chapters.title: State the boundary that must be preserved.
chapters.lead: The core concept helps explain a passage with its source context. Any adjacent offering should preserve a reviewable scope and avoid implying specialist verification it cannot provide.
chapters.body: An expansion could introduce new source, access or delivery requirements. Record those conditions before treating adjacency as low risk. The current scope is fictional and provides no evidence that the core offering itself is validated.
chapters.detail: Core work, audience and delivery assumptions remain open questions. The option list is not a licence to promise capabilities beyond the stated concept.
chapters.question: Which boundary would be hardest to preserve in a new task?

records.label: Core task
records.prompt: Explain a passage with relevant source context.

records.label: Protected condition
records.prompt: Keep scope and unresolved claims visible.

records.label: Validation gap
records.prompt: Even the core concept remains unvalidated.

chapters.title: Map five options without ranking a winner.
chapters.lead: O01 clarifies the core task. O02 explores a companion worksheet. O03 explores a team-use format. O04 examines an editorial-channel route. O05 considers a partner-led introduction.
chapters.body: The options have different learning questions and dependencies. Their teaching-token counts describe assumed effort, not strategic attractiveness or commercial return. A higher token count is neither a better opportunity nor proof of greater risk.
chapters.detail: Token needs are 2, 3, 5, 4 and 6, totalling 20 if all were explored. No approved resources are supplied.
chapters.question: Which option answers a question that matters before another option can be considered?

records.label: Core / adjacent
records.prompt: O01 core task; O02 companion worksheet.

records.label: New format / route
records.prompt: O03 team use; O04 editorial channel.

records.label: Partner option
records.prompt: O05 partner-led introduction, with permission unresolved.

chapters.title: Inspect an adjacent task before packaging it.
chapters.lead: A companion worksheet might help a reader connect a passage with a working question. It depends on understanding the core task, not simply reformatting existing copy.
chapters.body: O02 depends on O01 and uses three teaching tokens. A suitable exploration would examine the worksheet’s purpose and whether an existing practice already handles it. No reader test, product release or added value is established.
chapters.detail: Use an appropriate concept review before proposing a package or commercial arrangement. The worksheet remains a hypothesis about a task.
chapters.question: What would show that the worksheet does something worth keeping?

records.label: Dependency
records.prompt: O02 follows a suitable exploration of O01.

records.label: Learning question
records.prompt: Does the companion format clarify the task?

records.label: Resource assumption
records.prompt: 3 teaching tokens; not actual cost.

chapters.title: Treat a new group as an evidence gap.
chapters.lead: A team-use format may introduce coordination and review responsibilities absent from an individual task. Similar content does not establish a similar buying or use context.
chapters.body: O03 depends on O01 and O02 and uses five teaching tokens. Explore who would use, choose and review such a format before calling it a new customer segment or a revenue opportunity.
chapters.detail: There are no team interviews, adoption figures, shared-work permissions or commercial agreements in this example.
chapters.question: Which assumption changes most when the task moves from one person to a team?

records.label: User question
records.prompt: Who needs to explain and review the material?

records.label: Dependency
records.prompt: O01 and O02 must be considered first.

records.label: Evidence gap
records.prompt: No team demand or actual adoption supplied.

chapters.title: Design a channel experiment around understanding.
chapters.lead: An editorial-channel route could introduce the core concept through an explanation of a reader task. Its first question is whether the message reaches an appropriate context and is understood.
chapters.body: O04 depends on O01 and uses four teaching tokens. It does not establish a live channel, publication permission, traffic or conversion. Define a bounded observation before considering distribution at scale.
chapters.detail: Separate message delivery, comprehension and a commercial conversation. They are different observations with different limits.
chapters.question: What observation would justify continuing the channel inquiry?

records.label: Experiment question
records.prompt: Can an appropriate reader understand the core task?

records.label: Dependency
records.prompt: Clarify the core task through O01 first.

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: No live distribution or acquisition result supplied.

chapters.title: Compare resource combinations under a constraint.
chapters.lead: A teaching allowance of eight tokens cannot cover the twenty-token total. O01 plus O02 uses five, leaving three; that is not enough for O03, which requires another five.
chapters.body: O01 plus O04 uses six, leaving two, so O05 cannot follow within the same allowance because it needs six more. These examples illustrate constraints, not an approved portfolio or a recommendation about real resources.
chapters.detail: Do not choose the cheapest option merely because it fits. Relevant learning, dependency and actual responsibility still matter.
chapters.question: Which learning question is lost when the constraint rules out another option?

records.label: Route one
records.prompt: O01 + O02 = 5 tokens; 3 remain.

records.label: Route two
records.prompt: O01 + O04 = 6 tokens; 2 remain.

records.label: Constraint
records.prompt: 8 illustrative tokens cannot fund all 20.

chapters.title: Respect dependencies and permission questions.
chapters.lead: O02 and O04 depend on O01. O03 depends on O01 and O02. O05 depends on O04. These arrows express planning assumptions, not evidence that the sequence will cause growth.
chapters.body: The partner-led option also needs an appropriate relationship, permission and shared understanding of the offering. No partner commitment, endorsement or distribution authority is supplied.
chapters.detail: The source register is acyclic and inspectable. Revisit an edge when new information changes what must be learned first.
chapters.question: Which dependency is a learning need, and which requires an actual agreement?

records.label: Learning dependency
records.prompt: Clarify the core task before adapting the format.

records.label: Channel dependency
records.prompt: Understand O04 before considering O05.

records.label: Permission gap
records.prompt: No actual partner agreement or endorsement.

chapters.title: Set stop and revision rules in advance.
chapters.lead: A possible stop rule is that an option cannot explain a distinct task value after an appropriate review. Another is that a required permission or responsibility remains unavailable.
chapters.body: The rules are proposed learning conditions, not tested thresholds or automatic business decisions. Record inconclusive evidence separately from evidence against the option. Avoid continuing only because resources have already been used.
chapters.detail: No experiment has been completed and no option is a proven winner. A decision needs relevant evidence and the actual authority to interpret it.
chapters.question: What would make you stop rather than search for a more favourable story?

records.label: Continue question
records.prompt: Is the task value still credible and inspectable?

records.label: Revise condition
records.prompt: The current explanation misses the intended task.

records.label: Stop condition
records.prompt: An essential requirement cannot be responsibly satisfied.

chapters.title: Review the portfolio as a set of questions.
chapters.lead: After appropriate exploration, compare what each option taught and what remains unknown. An option may be useful because it invalidates a premise rather than because it produces an expansion.
chapters.body: The current register contains five untested options and no actual growth, return or experiment result. Preserve the original question and dependency when revising the portfolio so another reviewer can understand the change.
chapters.detail: A changed resource total does not establish a better strategy. Keep learning evidence, commercial assumptions and actual commitments distinct.
chapters.question: Which question should be retired, reframed or explored next?

records.label: Retain
records.prompt: The learning question and prior dependency assumptions.

records.label: Review
records.prompt: What appropriate evidence changes the option’s meaning?

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: No measured growth, return or approved investment.

title: OPERATING MODEL
subtitle: A capability, interface and responsibility system
scope: A fictional Source Desk operating-model proposal. Four roles and five interfaces are conceptual; no named appointments, delegated authority, service commitments or actual organisational process are supplied.

chapters.title: Start with the work the organisation would need to do.
chapters.lead: Source Desk is a fictional concept for coordinating source-based explanations. Its operating-model question is how a defined task could move between roles without losing context or responsibility.
chapters.body: An organisation chart alone cannot answer that question. This proposal examines capabilities, interfaces and review conditions. It establishes no actual team, appointments, operating authority or service commitments.
chapters.detail: The model uses four functional roles and five proposed interfaces. Keep each responsibility linked to the relevant task rather than assuming that a title grants permission.
chapters.question: What must remain clear when the work moves to another role?

records.label: Intent
records.prompt: Coordinate a bounded source-based explanation task.

records.label: Model scope
records.prompt: 4 conceptual roles and 5 proposed interfaces.

records.label: Authority boundary
records.prompt: No real appointments or delegated powers.

chapters.title: Trace a value flow that can return for clarification.
chapters.lead: The proposed flow moves from a scoped brief to a draft, a source-status note, a review question and a revised explanation. The final handoff returns to the owner for another scope check.
chapters.body: Return paths matter because review can create a question rather than an approval. The five interfaces are planning assumptions, not observed work or a guarantee that the process fits a real organisation.
chapters.detail: Each output becomes the next interface’s input. This continuity makes the model inspectable without claiming that any actual handoff has happened.
chapters.question: Where should an unresolved meaning return rather than disappear?

records.label: Start
records.prompt: Owner supplies a scoped brief to the author.

records.label: Review path
records.prompt: Draft, source-status note and review question.

records.label: Return
records.prompt: Revised explanation goes back for a scope check.

chapters.title: Map capabilities before assigning people.
chapters.lead: The work needs intake, explanation, source coordination, review and revision capabilities. A capability describes something the proposed system must be able to do, not a named person or a software feature.
chapters.body: One person might hold several roles in a real setting, but relevant responsibility and review boundaries must remain distinguishable. The model supplies no headcount, skill assessment or hiring plan.
chapters.detail: Ask what artifact makes each capability visible and what information it needs from another role. Do not treat a list of capabilities as evidence that they are available.
chapters.question: Which capability is assumed but not actually established?

records.label: Intake / explanation
records.prompt: Clarify the task and draft its meaning.

records.label: Coordination / review
records.prompt: Preserve source status and inspect the question.

records.label: Revision
records.prompt: Explain a change and return unresolved conditions.

chapters.title: Define interfaces as agreements about work.
chapters.lead: An interface should name the sender, receiver, input, expected output and unresolved condition. A transfer of a file is not automatically a transfer of understanding or authority.
chapters.body: The source register proposes owner to author, author to coordinator, coordinator to reviewer, reviewer to author and author to owner. No actual recipient, deadline or service agreement is supplied.
chapters.detail: Use an explicit receiving question to expose a gap. Received should not mean verified unless that meaning is actually agreed and supported.
chapters.question: What would let the receiver know what has and has not been checked?

records.label: Sender / receiver
records.prompt: A functional handoff, not a named appointment.

records.label: Artifact / question
records.prompt: Identify the version and requested next review.

records.label: Boundary
records.prompt: Receipt does not imply approval or delegated authority.

chapters.title: Carry context with the information.
chapters.lead: A draft should travel with its working question, source status and relevant version. If a condition is unresolved, keep it next to the claim rather than only in an unrelated message.
chapters.body: The operating model describes information needs, not an implemented system or permission to share material. Real access, retention and source-use arrangements require appropriate decisions in the actual setting.
chapters.detail: A source-status note can say that a source is missing. It must not make a gap appear resolved just to produce a complete-looking handoff.
chapters.question: Which piece of context would change how the next role interprets the draft?

records.label: Working question
records.prompt: Why this explanation is being prepared.

records.label: Source status
records.prompt: What is attributable and what remains unresolved.

records.label: Version
records.prompt: Which artifact the next role is actually reviewing.

chapters.title: Separate a proposal from delegated authority.
chapters.lead: The owner could define the task scope, the reviewer could inspect within an agreed remit and the author could revise the explanation. These are proposed responsibilities, not granted decision rights.
chapters.body: A real operating arrangement must establish who can approve, reject, refer or publish in the relevant context. Do not infer permission from a role label or from completion of a review worksheet.
chapters.detail: The source register marks all delegation as not granted. This is a planning boundary, not an assessment of an actual organisation’s governance.
chapters.question: Which decision needs a real authority that this document cannot provide?

records.label: Scope decision
records.prompt: Who can define or change the task?

records.label: Review decision
records.prompt: Who can judge the relevant claim and its evidence?

records.label: Release decision
records.prompt: Who can authorise the actual use or publication?

chapters.title: Allocate resources to capabilities, not just boxes.
chapters.lead: A proposed system needs time, suitable source access and appropriate review capability. Resource planning should consider the work at the interfaces, not only the visible production step.
chapters.body: No staffing levels, budget, workload or service duration are supplied. A role’s presence on the map does not establish its availability or imply that coordination and revision have no cost.
chapters.detail: Inspect shared constraints and supporting work before proposing commitments. A real allocation needs appropriate responsibility and relevant information.
chapters.question: Which interface could become constrained even if drafting capacity increased?

records.label: Time
records.prompt: Preparation, handoff, review and revision all need attention.

records.label: Information
records.prompt: Relevant source context must be appropriately available.

records.label: Capability
records.prompt: No actual staff availability or budget established.

chapters.title: Choose a review rhythm for a defined purpose.
chapters.lead: A useful rhythm might include a scope check before drafting, a source-status check before review and a revision check before another decision. Each should answer a specific question.
chapters.body: These are relative review points, not a calendar or a real meeting obligation. More meetings do not automatically create clearer responsibility. Decide what information should trigger a discussion and what can be handled through an appropriate artifact.
chapters.detail: The model provides no actual meeting dates, response times or service levels. Keep the rhythm adaptable to the task and the relevant access conditions.
chapters.question: Which review point would prevent a meaningful uncertainty from being hidden?

records.label: Before drafting
records.prompt: Is the task scope understandable?

records.label: Before review
records.prompt: Are source status and the receiving question visible?

records.label: After revision
records.prompt: What changed, and which condition remains open?

chapters.title: Handle a conflict at the relevant interface.
chapters.lead: If the author and reviewer interpret a claim differently, preserve both the question and the relevant source before deciding who should resolve it. Do not let a status label conceal the disagreement.
chapters.body: The model grants no escalation or arbitration power. A real concern needs an appropriate actual route and a clear remit. Distinguish missing information, competing interpretations and a decision that requires authority.
chapters.detail: Record the issue at the task level without unnecessary personal information or an assumed judgement about someone’s motives.
chapters.question: Is the conflict about a fact, an interpretation or who may decide?

records.label: Issue
records.prompt: The claim has competing interpretations.

records.label: Information needed
records.prompt: Relevant source, version and intended meaning.

records.label: Authority gap
records.prompt: No actual escalation or decision route supplied.

chapters.title: Evolve the model with a visible reason.
chapters.lead: When an interface changes, record what work moved, why the change was proposed and how responsibility and source context will remain inspectable. Preserve the earlier map for comparison.
chapters.body: This version contains a conceptual loop, not a tested organisational design. No actual performance improvement, governance approval or implemented change is reported. Use appropriate evidence before transferring the proposal into a real setting.
chapters.detail: A cleaner diagram is not proof of a better system. Review the work and its conditions, not merely the appearance of the model.
chapters.question: What evidence would justify changing this capability or interface?

records.label: Change record
records.prompt: Describe the proposed difference and its task reason.

records.label: Continuity check
records.prompt: Preserve the receiving question and responsibility boundary.

records.label: Implementation boundary
records.prompt: No real approval, rollout or measured improvement.
